title: Motivation and Teams
description: Motivation, coordination, and group dynamics at work.

questions.prompt: In self-determination theory, which needs support autonomous motivation?
questions.explanation: The theory highlights autonomy, competence, and relatedness; supporting these needs can foster more self-endorsed motivation.

questions.prompt: A performance bonus reliably increases intrinsic interest in every task.
questions.explanation: Effects of rewards depend on design and context; controlling rewards can sometimes undermine autonomy or intrinsic interest.

questions.prompt: Expectancy theory predicts motivation depends partly on whether effort seems likely to produce performance and valued outcomes.
questions.explanation: Expectancy, instrumentality, and valence are distinct links in the motivation process.

questions.prompt: Psychological safety is best described as a shared belief that:
options: No one will be held accountable
questions.explanation: Psychological safety supports speaking up and learning; it is not the absence of standards or disagreement.

questions.prompt: A cohesive team always makes better decisions than a less cohesive team.
questions.explanation: Cohesion can aid coordination but can also discourage dissent; decision quality depends on norms and information use.

questions.prompt: Which practices can improve team coordination?
questions.explanation: Explicit roles, goals, and dependency checks reduce coordination failures and hidden assumptions.

questions.prompt: Social loafing can occur when individual contributions are hard to identify in a group task.
questions.explanation: Reduced identifiability and accountability can lower effort, especially when members see their input as dispensable.

questions.prompt: A team’s shared mental model can help members anticipate one another’s needs.
questions.explanation: Shared understanding of tasks and roles can support coordination, especially in interdependent work.

questions.prompt: What is a useful response to groupthink risk?
questions.explanation: Independent input and explicit dissent reduce pressure to converge prematurely.

questions.prompt: Task conflict about ideas is always harmful to team performance.
questions.explanation: Constructive disagreement may improve decisions, but personal conflict and poorly managed debate can impair work.

questions.prompt: Which conditions support effective feedback?
options: A chance to discuss next steps
questions.explanation: Behavior-focused and actionable feedback is clearer and fairer than broad trait labels.

questions.prompt: Equity perceptions can depend on how people compare their inputs and outcomes with others.
questions.explanation: People assess fairness partly through social comparisons, though what counts as an input or outcome varies.

questions.prompt: A highly motivated employee can still underperform when necessary resources are missing.
questions.explanation: Motivation is not a substitute for ability, role clarity, opportunity, or tools.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a task interdependence?
options: One member’s output is needed for another’s work
A team shares a lunch break
questions.explanation: Task interdependence describes how members’ work or outputs rely on one another.

questions.prompt: Which norms can make meetings more inclusive?
options: Ask for written input before discussion
Allow interruption by the most senior person
questions.explanation: Structured turn-taking and advance input can broaden participation; accurately noting dissent prevents false consensus.

questions.prompt: Recognition is most useful when it is specific and connected to meaningful contribution.
questions.explanation: Specific recognition clarifies valued behaviors; sincerity and fairness matter more than generic praise.

questions.prompt: A team charter can clarify purpose, roles, decision rules, and communication expectations.
questions.explanation: A charter makes assumptions explicit and can be revisited when the team’s work changes.

questions.prompt: When team members disagree about facts, a strong first step is to:
options: Identify what evidence would resolve the disagreement
Treat the senior person’s view as evidence
questions.explanation: Agreeing on relevant evidence can turn an unproductive dispute into a testable question.

questions.prompt: Which can reduce free-riding in group work?
options: Connect individual work to shared outcomes
questions.explanation: Visibility, manageable size, and meaningful accountability help members see how their contributions matter.

questions.prompt: Team effectiveness should be judged only by short-term output.
questions.explanation: Effectiveness also includes quality, adaptability, member well-being, and capacity to work together in the future.
